beats.role_note: COLD OPEN -- required fellow intro line + AI-voice disclosure; the question
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Boopesh M., and this video is about explainable AI in lending. When an AI credit model says no to a loan, why did it say no? Quick note: this is an AI voice reading my script. And every number comes from my own small experiment, on synthetic applicants.

props.command: When an AI credit model denies a loan, how do you find the specific reasons it said no?
output: synthetic applicants: 20,000 made up, 5 plain features
Applicant A: denied by a scorecard and by a black-box model
top 3 reasons from each model: they share 2 of 3

beats.role_note: BLUF -- hesitant writer corrects the misconception
beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one line. The model said no is not a reason. A lender has to name the facts that drove the no.

props.text: You were denied because the model said no.
props.replacementWords: your debt is too high for your income

contextItems.label: The catch
contextItems.detail: a black box has no weights to read

beats.role_note: Reg B 1002.9(b)(2): specific principal reasons; 'failed a score' insufficient; CFPB Circular 2022-03 (withdrawn May 2025); not legal advice
beats.narration_text: First, the rule. In the US, Regulation B, under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, says a denied applicant gets specific reasons: the principal ones. You failed to reach our score is not enough. In twenty twenty-two, a CFPB circular said this holds for complex algorithms too. It was withdrawn in twenty twenty-five, but the regulation's wording remains. That's what the rule asks for, not legal advice.

beats.role_note: 20,000 synthetic applicants, 5 features, no protected traits; scorecard vs boosted; same AUC
beats.narration_text: Now my experiment: twenty thousand synthetic applicants, with five plain features: income, debt-to-income, missed payments, credit history length, and card use. No protected traits; fairness is another video. I trained two models: a simple scorecard, and a gradient-boosted black box. On test data, both rank risk equally well.

beats.role_note: A's five values; risk 53 % (scorecard) vs 34 % (boosted) vs cutoff 30 %; both deny
beats.narration_text: Meet Applicant A, also made up. Debt payments take forty-four percent of income. Cards are seventy-two percent used. One missed payment, four years of history. My chosen line is a thirty percent risk of default. The scorecard puts A at fifty-three percent; the black box, at thirty-four. Both say no.

beats.role_note: one formula: push = weight x (A - average); bars; top 3 dti / util / missed
beats.narration_text: Why? For the scorecard, the answer is exact. Each feature's push toward no is its weight, times how far A sits from the average applicant. Five multiplications. The top three reasons: debt payments too high for income, cards near their limits, and a recent missed payment.

beats.role_note: Shapley values, 16,000 model runs; top 3 missed / util / history; 2 of 3 shared; reasons shift with comparison group / retraining
beats.narration_text: The black box has no weights to read. So I computed Shapley values: swap A's features in and out, in every combination, against five hundred other applicants. Sixteen thousand model runs, for one person. Its top three: the missed payment, card use, and a short credit history. Two of three match the scorecard. And the list can shift: compare A with approved applicants only, or retrain, and debt-to-income moves back into its top three.

beats.role_note: counterfactual: pay cards down $3,850 (72 % -> 34 %), both approve; limits
beats.narration_text: So, what would change the answer? Keep everything else, and pay card balances down by about three thousand eight hundred dollars, from seventy-two to thirty-four percent of the limit. Both models now say yes. That's the kind of reason a person can act on. Limits: synthetic applicants, a cutoff I chose, and Shapley values are one method among several.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude, with my script attached. Retrain the black box with a different seed. Does Applicant A keep the same top three reasons?

props.command: Here's my script (credit_reasons.py). Train a second boosted model with a different seed and data split. Does Applicant A get the same top 3 reasons? How often do the top 3 change across 20 seeds? Show the numbers.
